Vice President-elect Humphrey alongside [Coretta Scott King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coretta_Scott_King "Coretta Scott King") and civil rights leader Dr. [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.") in 1964.

### Vice presidential campaign

Further information: [1964 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection "1964 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection") and [Lyndon B. Johnson 1964 presidential campaign §Democratic national convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson_1964_presidential_campaign#Democratic_national_convention "Lyndon B. Johnson 1964 presidential campaign")

Humphrey's defeat in 1960 had a profound influence on his thinking; after the primaries he told friends that, as a relatively poor man in politics, he was unlikely to ever become president unless he served as vice president first.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolberg1984240-117) Humphrey believed that only in this way could he attain the funds, nationwide organization, and visibility he would need to win the Democratic nomination. So as the [1964 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_United_States_presidential_election "1964 United States presidential election") began, Humphrey made clear his interest in becoming Lyndon Johnson's running mate. At the [1964 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Democratic_National_Convention "1964 Democratic National Convention"), Johnson kept the three likely vice-presidential candidates, Connecticut Senator [Thomas Dodd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_J._Dodd "Thomas J. Dodd"), fellow Minnesota Senator [Eugene McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_McCarthy "Eugene McCarthy"), and Humphrey,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-118) as well as the rest of the nation, in suspense before announcing his choice of Humphrey with much fanfare, praising his qualifications at considerable length before announcing his name.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-119)

The following day Humphrey's acceptance speech overshadowed Johnson's own acceptance address:

> Hubert warmed up with a long tribute to the President, then hit his stride as he began a rhythmic jabbing and chopping at [Barry Goldwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Goldwater "Barry Goldwater"). "Most Democrats and Republicans in the Senate voted for an $11.5 billion tax cut for American citizens and American business," he cried, "but not Senator Goldwater. Most Democrats and Republicans in the Senate – in fact four-fifths of the members of his own party – voted for the Civil Rights Act, but not Senator Goldwater." Time after time, he capped his indictments with the drumbeat cry: "But not Senator Goldwater!" The delegates caught the cadence and took up the chant. A quizzical smile spread across Humphrey's face, then turned to a laugh of triumph. Hubert was in fine form. He knew it. The delegates knew it. And no one could deny that Hubert Humphrey would be a formidable political antagonist in the weeks ahead.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-120)

In an address before labor leaders in [Youngstown, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youngstown,_Ohio "Youngstown, Ohio"), on September 7, 1964, Humphrey said the labor movement had "more at stake in this election than almost any other segment of society".[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-121) In [Jamesburg, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamesburg,_New_Jersey "Jamesburg, New Jersey"), on September 10, Humphrey remarked that Goldwater had a "record of retreat and reaction" when it came to issues of urban housing.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-122) During a September 12 [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver") Democratic rally, Humphrey charged Goldwater with having rejected programs that most Americans and members of his own party supported.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-123) At a [Santa Fe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Fe,_New_Mexico "Santa Fe, New Mexico") September 13 rally, Humphrey said the Goldwater-led Republican Party was seeking "to divide America so that they may conquer" and that Goldwater would pinch individuals in his reduction of government.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-124) On September 16, Humphrey said the [Americans for Democratic Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans_for_Democratic_Action "Americans for Democratic Action") supported the Johnson administration's economic sanctions against Cuba, and that the organization wanted to see a free Cuban government.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-125) The following day in [San Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio "San Antonio"), Texas, Humphrey said Goldwater opposed programs favored by most Texans and Americans.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-126) During a September 27 appearance in [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland"), Ohio, Humphrey said the Kennedy administration had led America in a prosperous direction and called for voters to issue a referendum with their vote against "those who seek to replace the Statue of Liberty with an iron-padlocked gate."[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-127) At an October 1 rally in [Tacoma, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma,_Washington "Tacoma, Washington"), Humphrey attacked Goldwater as a radical who opposed the 1960 GOP platform and true conservatism, which in Humphrey's opinion meant a balance of tradition and progress.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-128)

At Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles, California, on October 2, Humphrey said the general election would give voters a choice between his running mate and a candidate "who curses the darkness and never lights a candle".[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-129) During an October 9 [Jersey City, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_City,_New_Jersey "Jersey City, New Jersey"), appearance, Humphrey responded to critics of the administration, who he called "sick and tired Americans", by touting the accomplishments of both Kennedy's and Johnson's presidencies.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-130) In [Tampa, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa,_Florida "Tampa, Florida"), on October 18, a week after the resignation of [Walter Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Jenkins "Walter Jenkins") amid a scandal, Humphrey said he was unaware of any potential security leaks relating to the case.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-131) In [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") on October 24, Humphrey listed the censure vote toward Senator [Joseph McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_McCarthy "Joseph McCarthy"), the civil rights bill, and the nuclear test ban treaty as "three great issues of conscience to come before the United States Senate in the past decade" that Goldwater had voted incorrectly on as a Senator.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-132) In an October 26 speech in Chicago, Humphrey called Goldwater "neither a Republican nor a Democrat" and "a radical".[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-133)

The Johnson-Humphrey ticket won the election overwhelmingly, with 486 electoral votes out of 538.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-134) Only five Southern states and Goldwater's home state of Arizona supported the Republican ticket.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-135) In October Humphrey had predicted that the ticket would win by a large margin but not carry every state.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-136)

### Vice President-elect of the United States

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/President_Lyndon_B._Johnson_and_Vice-President-Elect_Hubert_Humphrey_%28436-253-wh64%29.jpg/250px-President_Lyndon_B._Johnson_and_Vice-President-Elect_Hubert_Humphrey_%28436-253-wh64%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Lyndon_B._Johnson_and_Vice-President-Elect_Hubert_Humphrey_(436-253-wh64).jpg)

Humphrey (right) horse-riding with President Johnson (left) at the [LBJ ranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LBJ_Ranch "LBJ Ranch"), c.November 4, 1964

Soon after winning the election, Humphrey and Johnson went to [LBJ ranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LBJ_Ranch "LBJ Ranch") near [Stonewall, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall,_Texas "Stonewall, Texas").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-137) On November 6, 1964, Humphrey traveled to the [Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Islands "Virgin Islands") for a two-week vacation.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-138) News stations aired taped remarks in which Humphrey stated that he had not discussed with Johnson what his role would be as vice president and that national campaigns should be reduced by four weeks.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-139) In a November 20 interview, Humphrey announced he would resign his Senate seat midway through the next month so that [Walter Mondale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Mondale "Walter Mondale") could assume the position.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-140)

On December 10, 1964, Humphrey met with Johnson in the Oval Office, the latter charging the vice president-elect with "developing a publicity machine extraordinaire and of always wanting to get his name in the paper." Johnson showed Humphrey a George Reed memo with the allegation that the president would die within six months from an already acquired fatal heart disease.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-141) The same day, during a speech in Washington, Johnson announced Humphrey would have the position of giving assistance to governmental civil rights programs.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-142)

On January 19, 1965, the day before the inauguration, Humphrey told the [Democratic National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") that the party had unified because of the national consensus established by the presidential election.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-143)

## Vice presidency (1965–1969)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Hubert_Humphrey_1965.jpg/250px-Hubert_Humphrey_1965.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hubert_Humphrey_1965.jpg)

Vice President Humphrey at a meeting in the [Oval Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oval_Office "Oval Office"), c.June 21, 1965

Humphrey took office on January 20, 1965,[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-144) ending the 14-month vacancy of the vice president of the United States, which had remained empty when then-Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson assumed the presidency after the [assassination of John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") in November 1963.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-145) He was an early skeptic of the then growing [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). Following a successful [Viet Cong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viet_Cong "Viet Cong") hit-and-run [attack on a U.S. military installation at Pleiku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Camp_Holloway "Attack on Camp Holloway") on February 7, 1965 (where 7 Americans were killed and 109 wounded), Humphrey returned from Georgia to Washington D.C., to attempt to prevent further escalation.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-T._Hoopes,_p31-146) He told President Johnson that bombing [North Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vietnam "North Vietnam") was not a solution to the problems in [South Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Vietnam "South Vietnam"), but that bombing would require the injection of US ground forces into South Vietnam to protect the airbases.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-T._Hoopes,_p31-146) Presciently, he noted that a military solution in Vietnam would take several years, well beyond the next election cycle. In response to this advice, President Johnson punished Humphrey by treating him coldly and restricting him from his inner circle for a number of months, until Humphrey decided to "get back on the team" and fully support the war effort.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-T._Hoopes,_p31-146)

As vice president, Humphrey was criticized for his complete and vocal loyalty to Johnson and the policies of the Johnson administration, even as many of his liberal admirers opposed the president's policies with increasing fervor regarding the Vietnam War.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Humphrey_Wilson_Center-23) Many of Humphrey's liberal friends and allies abandoned him because of his refusal to publicly criticize Johnson's Vietnam War policies. Humphrey's critics later learned that Johnson had threatened Humphrey – Johnson told Humphrey that if he publicly criticized his policies, he would destroy Humphrey's chances to become president by opposing his nomination at the next Democratic Convention.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolberg1984282%E2%80%93284-147) However, Humphrey's critics were vocal and persistent: even his nickname, "the Happy Warrior", was used against him. The nickname referred not to his military hawkishness, but rather to his crusading for social welfare and civil rights programs.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Humphrey_Wilson_Center-23) After his narrow defeat in the 1968 presidential election, Humphrey wrote that "After four years as Vice-President ... I had lost some of my personal identity and personal forcefulness. ... I ought not to have let a man [Johnson] who was going to be a former President dictate my future."[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolberg1984407-148)

While he was vice president, Hubert Humphrey was the subject of a satirical song by songwriter/musician [Tom Lehrer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Lehrer "Tom Lehrer") entitled "Whatever Became of Hubert?" The song addressed how some liberals and [progressives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism "Progressivism") felt let down by Humphrey, who had become a much more mute figure as vice president than he had been as a senator. The song goes _"Whatever became of Hubert? Has anyone heard a thing? Once he shone on his own, now he sits home alone and waits for the phone to ring. Once a fiery liberal spirit, ah, but now when he speaks he must clear it. ..."_

During these years Humphrey was a repeated and favorite guest of [Johnny Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Carson "Johnny Carson") on _[The Tonight Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tonight\_Show "The Tonight Show")_.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-149)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-150) He also struck up a friendship with [Frank Sinatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sinatra "Frank Sinatra"), who supported his campaign for president in 1968 before his conversion to the Republican party in the early 1970s,[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-151) and was perhaps most on notice in the fall of 1977 when Sinatra was the star attraction and host of a tribute to a then-ailing Humphrey. He also appeared on _[The Dean Martin Celebrity Roast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dean\_Martin\_Celebrity\_Roast "The Dean Martin Celebrity Roast")_ in 1973.

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Gemini_4_Astronauts_Meet_Yuri_Gagarin.jpg/250px-Gemini_4_Astronauts_Meet_Yuri_Gagarin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gemini_4_Astronauts_Meet_Yuri_Gagarin.jpg)

Humphrey with Soviet cosmonaut [Yuri Gagarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin "Yuri Gagarin") and [Gemini 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini") astronauts at the 1965 [Paris Air Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Air_Show "Paris Air Show")

On April 15, 1965, Humphrey delivered an address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, pledging the incumbent session of Congress would "do more for the lasting long-term health of this nation" since the initial session in office at the time of [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") assuming the presidency in 1933 and predicting 13 major measures of President Johnson's administration would be passed ahead of the session's conclusion.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-152) In mid-May 1965, Humphrey traveled to [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), Texas for an off-the-record discussion with donors of President Johnson's campaign. During the visit, Humphrey was imposed tight security as a result of the JFK assassination a year and a half prior and the mother of [Lee Harvey Oswald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Harvey_Oswald "Lee Harvey Oswald") was placed under surveillance by Police Chief Cato Hightower.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-153)

During a May 31, 1966, appearance at Huron College, Humphrey said the U.S. should not expect "either friendship or gratitude" in helping poorer countries.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-154) At a September 22, 1966 [Jamesburg, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamesburg,_New_Jersey "Jamesburg, New Jersey") Democratic Party fundraiser, Humphrey said the Vietnam War would be shortened if the US stayed firm and hastened the return of troops: "We are making a decision not only to defend Vietnam, we are defending the United States of America."[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-155)

During a May 1967 news conference, Humphrey said American anger toward Vietnam was losing traction and that he could see a growth in popularity for President Johnson since a low point five months prior.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-156) During an August 2, 1967, appearance in [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit"), Humphrey proposed each state consider forming peacekeeping councils focused on preventing violence, gaining community cooperation, and listening to "the voices of those who have gone unheard."[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-157)

On November 4, 1967, Humphrey cited [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia") as an example of what Vietnam could resemble post a Viet Cong defeat while in [Jakarta, Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta,_Indonesia "Jakarta, Indonesia").[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-158) The following day, Vice President Humphrey requested Indonesia attempt mediation in the Vietnam War during a meeting with [Suharto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suharto "Suharto") at Merdeka palace.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-159) On December 7, Vice President Humphrey said in an interview that the Viet Cong could potentially be the factor in creating a political compromise with the government of Saigon.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-160)

### Civil rights

In February 1965, President Johnson appointed Humphrey to the chairmanship of the President's Council on Equal Opportunity.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Dallek224-161) The position and board had been proposed by Humphrey, who told Johnson that the board should consist of members of the Cabinet and federal agency leaders and serve multiple roles: assisting agency cooperation, creating federal program consistency, using advanced planning to avoid potential racial unrest, creating public policy, and meeting with local and state level leaders.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Thurber171-162) During his tenure, he appointed [Wiley A Branton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiley_A_Branton "Wiley A Branton") as executive director.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-163) During the first meeting of the group on March 3, Humphrey stated the budget was US$289,000 and pledged to ensure vigorous work by the small staff.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Thurber171-162) Following the [Watts riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts_riots "Watts riots") in August of that year, Johnson downsized Humphrey's role as the administration's expert on civil rights. Dallek wrote the shift in role was in line with the change in policy the Johnson administration underwent in response to "the changing political mood in the country on aid to African Americans."[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Dallek224-161) In a private meeting with Joseph Califano on September 18, 1965, President Johnson stated his intent to remove Humphrey from the post of "point man" on civil rights within the administration, believing the vice president was tasked with enough work.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-164) Days later, Humphrey met with Johnson, Attorney General [Nicholas Katzenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Katzenbach "Nicholas Katzenbach"), and [White House Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Counsel "White House Counsel")[Lee C. White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_C._White "Lee C. White"). Johnson told Humphrey he would shorten his role within the administration's civil rights policies and pass a portion to Katzenbach, Califano writing that Humphrey agreed to go along with the plan reluctantly.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-165)

In an August 1967 speech at a county officials national convention in Detroit, Humphrey called for the establishment of a [Marshall Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Plan "Marshall Plan") that would curb poverty in the United States as well as address racial violence, and advocated for the creation of civil peace councils that would counter rioting. He said the councils should include representation from all minority groups and religions, state governments, the National Guard, and law enforcement agencies and that the United States would see itself out of trouble only when law and order was reestablished.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-166)

### Foreign trips

December 1965 saw the beginning of Humphrey's tour of eastern countries, saying he hoped to have "cordial and frank discussions" ahead of the trip beginning when asked about the content of the talks.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-167) During a December 29 meeting with [Prime Minister of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Japan "Prime Minister of Japan")[Eisaku Satō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisaku_Sat%C5%8D "Eisaku Satō"), Humphrey asked the latter for support on achieving peace in the Vietnam War and said it was a showing of strength that the United States wanted a peaceful ending rather than a display of weakness.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-168)

Humphrey began a European tour in late-March 1967 to mend frazzled relations and indicated that he was "ready to explain and ready to listen."[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-169) On April 2, 1967, Vice President Humphrey met with [Prime Minister of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom")[Harold Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Wilson "Harold Wilson"). Ahead of the meeting, Humphrey said they would discuss multiple topics including the nuclear nonproliferation treaty, European events, Atlantic alliance strengthening, and "the situation in the Far East".[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-170) White House Press Secretary [George Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Christian_(journalist) "George Christian (journalist)") said five days later that he had received reports from Vice President Humphrey indicating his tour of the European countries was "very constructive" and said President Johnson was interested in the report as well.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-171) While Humphrey was in [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), Italy on April 1, 1967, 23-year-old Giulio Stocchi threw eggs at the Vice President and missed. He was seized by American bodyguards who turned him in to Italian officers.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-172) In [Brussels, Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels,_Belgium "Brussels, Belgium") on April 9, demonstrators led by communists threw rotten eggs and fruits at Vice President Humphrey's car, also hitting several of his bodyguards.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-173) In late-December 1967, Vice President Humphrey began touring Africa.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-174)

### 1968 presidential campaign

Main articles: [Hubert Humphrey 1968 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey_1968_presidential_campaign "Hubert Humphrey 1968 presidential campaign") and [1968 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_United_States_presidential_election "1968 United States presidential election")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Hubert_Humphrey_and_Lyndon_Johnson.jpg/250px-Hubert_Humphrey_and_Lyndon_Johnson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hubert_Humphrey_and_Lyndon_Johnson.jpg)

Vice President Hubert Humphrey, President [Lyndon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_Johnson "Lyndon Johnson"), and General [Creighton Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_Abrams "Creighton Abrams") in a Cabinet Room meeting in March 1968

As 1968 began, it looked as if President Johnson, despite the rapidly decreasing approval rating of his Vietnam War policies, would easily win the Democratic nomination for a second time.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-175) Humphrey was widely expected to remain as Johnson's running mate for reelection in 1968.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-176) Johnson was challenged by Senator [Eugene McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_McCarthy "Eugene McCarthy") of Minnesota, who ran on an [anti-Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_to_the_U.S._involvement_in_the_Vietnam_War "Opposition to the U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War") platform.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-177) With the backing of out-of-state anti-war college students and activists while campaigning in the [New Hampshire primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hampshire_primary "New Hampshire primary"), McCarthy, who was not expected to be a serious contender for the Democratic nomination, nearly defeated Johnson, finishing with a surprising 42% of the vote to Johnson's 49%.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-178) A few days after the New Hampshire primary, after months of contemplation and originally intending to support Johnson's bid for reelection, Senator [Robert F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy "Robert F. Kennedy") of New York also entered the race on an anti-war platform.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-179) On March 31, a week before the Wisconsin primary, where polls showed a strong standing for McCarthy, Johnson stunned the nation by [withdrawing from his race for a second full term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Lyndon_B._Johnson_from_the_1968_United_States_presidential_election "Withdrawal of Lyndon B. Johnson from the 1968 United States presidential election").[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-180)

Humphrey announced his presidential candidacy on April 27.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-181) Declaring his candidacy in a speech in Washington, D.C. alongside Senators [Fred Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_R._Harris "Fred R. Harris") of [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma") and [Walter Mondale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Mondale "Walter Mondale") of Minnesota (who both served as the co-chairs to his campaign), Humphrey stated:

> Here we are, just as we ought to be, here we are, the people, here we are the spirit of dedication, here we are the way politics ought to be in America, the politics of happiness, politics of purpose, politics of joy; and that's the way it's going to be, all the way, too, from here on out. We seek an America able to preserve and nurture all the basic rights of free expression, yet able to reach across the divisions that too often separate race from race, region from region, young from old, worker from scholar, rich from poor. We seek an America able to do this in the higher knowledge that our goals and ideals are worthy of conciliation and personal sacrifice.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-UCSB_Remarks_Declaring_Candidacy-182)

Also in his speech, Humphrey supported Johnson's Vietnam initiative, which Johnson had proposed during his address to the nation four weeks earlier;[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-UCSB_Remarks_Declaring_Candidacy-182) partially halting the bombings in North Vietnam, while sending an additional 13,500 troops and increasing the [Department of Defense's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") budget by 4% over the next fiscal year.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-183) Later in the campaign, Humphrey opposed a proposal by Senators McCarthy and [George McGovern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_McGovern "George McGovern") of [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota") to the Democratic Convention's Policy Committee, calling for an immediate end to the bombings in Vietnam, an early withdrawal of troops and setting talks for a [coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_government "Coalition government") with the Viet Cong.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-184)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Photograph_of_Hubert_Humphrey_and_Edmund_Muskie_at_the_1968_Democratic_National_Convention_a.jpg/250px-Photograph_of_Hubert_Humphrey_and_Edmund_Muskie_at_the_1968_Democratic_National_Convention_a.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photograph_of_Hubert_Humphrey_and_Edmund_Muskie_at_the_1968_Democratic_National_Convention_a.jpg)

Vice President Humphrey (left) and U.S. Senator [Edmund Muskie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Muskie "Edmund Muskie") (right) wave from the podium at the [1968 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Democratic_National_Convention "1968 Democratic National Convention") in Chicago.

Many people saw Humphrey as Johnson's stand-in; he won major backing from the nation's labor unions and other Democratic groups troubled by young antiwar protesters and the social unrest around the nation.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-HHH_Papers-185) A group of British journalists wrote that Humphrey, despite his liberal record on civil rights and support for a nuclear test-ban treaty, "had turned into an arch-apologist for the war, who was given to trotting around Vietnam looking more than a little silly in olive-drab fatigues and a forage cap. The man whose name had been a by-word in the South for softness toward Negroes had taken to lecturing black groups ... the wild-eyed reformer had become the natural champion of every conservative element in the Democratic Party."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Chester,_p._147-89) Humphrey entered the race too late to participate in the [Democratic primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries,_1968 "Democratic Party presidential primaries, 1968")[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-186) and concentrated on winning delegates in non-primary states by gaining the support of Democratic officeholders who were elected delegates to the Democratic Convention.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-HHH_Papers-185) By June, McCarthy won in Oregon and Pennsylvania, while Kennedy had won in Indiana and Nebraska, though Humphrey was the front runner as he led the delegate count.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-HHH_Papers-185)[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-OMCA-187) The California primary was crucial for [Kennedy's campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_presidential_campaign,_1968 "Robert F. Kennedy presidential campaign, 1968"), as a McCarthy victory would have prevented Kennedy from reaching the number of delegates required to secure the nomination.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-OMCA-187) On June 4, Kennedy defeated McCarthy by less than 4% in the winner-take-all California primary.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-188) But the nation was shocked yet again when [Senator Kennedy was assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_assassination "Robert F. Kennedy assassination") after his victory speech at the [Ambassador Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador_Hotel_(Los_Angeles) "Ambassador Hotel (Los Angeles)") in Los Angeles.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-189) After the assassination of Kennedy, Humphrey suspended his campaign for two weeks.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolberg1984341-190)

#### Chicago riots and party fallout

Humphrey did not enter any of the 13 state primary elections,[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-191) but secured the Democratic nomination at the [national convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Democratic_National_Convention "1968 Democratic National Convention") in Chicago. Although antiwar candidates won most primary votes, party delegates adopted the nomination outcome and rejected the convention's proposed peace plank by 1,567+3⁄4 to 1,041+1⁄4.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGitlin1987331-192) Humphrey selected U.S. Senator [Ed Muskie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Muskie "Ed Muskie") of [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine") as his running mate.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

During the convention, thousands of [antiwar demonstrators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_to_the_Vietnam_War "Opposition to the Vietnam War") gathered in [Grant Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Park_(Chicago) "Grant Park (Chicago)")—about five miles south of the [International Amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Amphitheatre "International Amphitheatre")—and in other locations near downtown Chicago. In widely covered confrontations, [Mayor Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley")'s police forces used force against demonstrators, many of them young people and students, intensifying public attention to disorder and division surrounding the convention.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/ElectoralCollege1968.svg/250px-ElectoralCollege1968.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1968.svg)

1968 presidential election results

Humphrey's response to the unrest, Johnson's and Daley's behind-the-scenes efforts,[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGitlin1987331-192) and criticism that he won the nomination without competing in primaries contributed to tension within the party. Humphrey also declined to fully adopt [Eugene McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_McCarthy "Eugene McCarthy")'s proposals, and McCarthy did not offer an unqualified endorsement, further weakening Democratic unity. The climate of 1968—including President Johnson's unpopularity and the assassinations of [Robert F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy "Robert F. Kennedy") and [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.")—also shaped the general-election campaign. As [American Independent Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Independent_Party "American Independent Party") candidate [George Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wallace "George Wallace") later lost support among some white union voters, Humphrey narrowed the gap in polls, revised his Vietnam stance by calling for peace talks, and regained some support among antiwar Democrats.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-193)

Nixon won the electoral college and the election. Humphrey lost the [popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_United_States_presidential_election "1968 United States presidential election") by less than one percentage point, with 43.4% for Nixon (31,783,783 votes) to 42.7% (31,271,839) for Humphrey and 13.5% (9,901,118) for Wallace. Humphrey carried 13 states and the District of Columbia for 191 electoral votes, Nixon carried 32 states for 301 electoral votes, and Wallace carried five states for 46 electoral votes. In his concession speech, Humphrey said, "I have done my best. I have lost; Mr. Nixon has won. The democratic process has worked its will."[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-194)

## Post-vice presidency (1969–1978)

### Teaching and return to the Senate

See also: [Minnesota's congressional delegations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota's_congressional_delegations "Minnesota's congressional delegations")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/CarterandHumphrey.png/250px-CarterandHumphrey.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CarterandHumphrey.png)

Senator Humphrey with Democratic presidential nominee [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter"), in 1976. California Governor [Jerry Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Brown "Jerry Brown") is at right.

After leaving the vice presidency, Humphrey taught at [Macalester College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macalester_College "Macalester College") and the [University of Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota "University of Minnesota"), and served as chairman of the board of consultants at the [Encyclopædia Britannica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica "Encyclopædia Britannica") Educational Corporation.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

On February 11, 1969, Humphrey met privately with Mayor [Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley") and denied ever being "at war" with Daley during a press conference later in the day.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-195) In March, Humphrey declined to answer questions on the Johnson administration being either involved or privy to the cessation of bombing of North Vietnam during an interview on _[Issues and Answers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issues\_and\_Answers "Issues and Answers")_.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-196) At a press conference on June 2, 1969, Humphrey backed Nixon's peace efforts, dismissing the notion that he was not seeking an end to the war.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-197) In early July, Humphrey traveled to Finland for a private visit.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-198) Later that month, Humphrey returned to Washington after visiting Europe, a week after McCarthy declared he would not seek reelection, Humphrey declining to comment amid speculation he intended to return to the Senate.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-199) During the fall, Humphrey arranged to meet with President Nixon through [United States National Security Advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Security_Advisor "United States National Security Advisor")[Henry Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger "Henry Kissinger"), Humphrey saying the day after the meeting that Nixon had "expressed his appreciation on my attitude to his effort on Vietnam."[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolberg1984417-200) On August 3, Humphrey said that Russia was buying time to develop ballistic missile warheads to catch up with the United States and that security was the "overriding concern" of the Soviet Union.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-201) Days later, Humphrey repudiated efforts against Nixon's anti-ballistic missile system: "I have a feeling that they [opponents of the ABM] were off chasing rabbits when a tiger is loose."[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-202) During October, Humphrey spoke before the AFL-CIO convention delegates, charging Nixon's economic policies with "putting Americans out of work without slowing inflation."[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-203) On October 10, Humphrey stated his support for Nixon's policies in Vietnam and that he believed "the worst thing that we can do is to try to undermine the efforts of the President."[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-204) At a December 21 press conference, Humphrey said Nixon was a participant in the "politics of polarization" and could not seek unity on one hand but have divisive agents on the other.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-205) On December 26, Humphrey responded to a claim from former President Johnson that Humphrey had been cost the election by his own call for a stop to the bombing in North Vietnam, saying he did what he "thought was right and responsible at Salt Lake City."[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-206)

On January 4, 1970, Humphrey said the United States should cease tests of nuclear weapons during the continued conversations for potential strategic arms limitations between the United States and the Soviet Union while speaking to the National Retail Furniture Association.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-207) In February, Humphrey predicted Nixon would withdraw 75,000 or more troops prior to the year's midterm elections and the main issue would be the economy during an interview: "The issue of 1970 is the economy. Some of my fellow Democrats don't believe this. But this is a fact."[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-208) On February 23, Humphrey disclosed his recommendation that [Larry O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_O'Brien "Larry O'Brien") return as Chair of the [Democratic National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee"), a Humphrey spokesman reporting that he wanted the issue of the DNC chairmanship settled quickly.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-209) Solberg wrote that Nixon's April 1970 [Cambodian Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_Campaign "Cambodian Campaign") quashed Humphrey's hopes that the war be taken out of political context.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolberg1984417-200) In May, Humphrey pledged to do all he could to provide additional war planes to Israel and stress the issue to American leaders.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-210) Amid an August 11 address to an American Bar Association luncheon meeting, Humphrey called for liberals to cease defending campus radicals and militants and align with law and order.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-211)

Humphrey had not planned to return to political life, but saw an opportunity when McCarthy did not seek reelection in [the 1970 midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_United_States_Senate_election_in_Minnesota "1970 United States Senate election in Minnesota"). (McCarthy recognized that his opposition to Johnson and Humphrey had angered much of his party, making his renomination unlikely.) Humphrey won the nomination, defeated Republican Congressman [Clark MacGregor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_MacGregor "Clark MacGregor"), and returned to the U.S. Senate on January 3, 1971. Before resuming his duties, Humphrey had a November 16, 1970, White House meeting with Nixon as part of a group of newly elected senators.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-212) He was reelected in [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_U.S._Senate_election "1976 U.S. Senate election") and remained in office until his death. In a rarity in politics, Humphrey held both Senate seats from his state (Class I and Class II) at different times. During his return to the Senate he served in the [92nd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/92nd_United_States_Congress "92nd United States Congress"), [93rd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/93rd_United_States_Congress "93rd United States Congress"), [94th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/94th_United_States_Congress "94th United States Congress"), and part of the [95th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/95th_United_States_Congress "95th United States Congress"). He chaired the [Joint Economic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress_Joint_Economic_Committee "United States Congress Joint Economic Committee") in the 94th Congress.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Fourth Senate term

L. Edward Purcell wrote that upon returning to the Senate, Humphrey found himself "again a lowly junior senator with no seniority" and that he resolved to create credibility in the eyes of liberals.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-213) On May 3, 1971, after the [Americans for Democratic Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans_for_Democratic_Action "Americans for Democratic Action") adopted a resolution demanding Nixon's impeachment, Humphrey said they were acting "more out of emotion and passion than reason and prudent judgment" and that the request was irresponsible.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-214) On May 21, Humphrey said ending hunger and malnutrition in the U.S. was "a moral obligation" during a speech to International Food Service Manufacturers Association members.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-215) In June, Humphrey delivered the commencement address at the [University of Bridgeport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bridgeport "University of Bridgeport")[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-216) and days later said that he believed Nixon was interested in seeing a peaceful end to the Vietnam War "as badly as any senator or anybody else."[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-217) On July 14, testifying before the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee on Arms Control, Humphrey proposed amending the defense procurement bill to place in escrow all funds for creation and usage of multiple‐missile warheads in the midst of continued arms limitations talks. Humphrey said members of the Nixon administration needed to remember "when they talk of a tough negotiating position, they are going to get a tough response."[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-218) On September 6, Humphrey rebuked the Nixon administration's wage price freeze, saying it was based on trickle-down policies and advocating "percolate up" as a replacement, while speaking at a [United Rubber Workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Rubber_Workers "United Rubber Workers") gathering.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-219) On October 26, Humphrey stated his support for removing barriers to voting registration and authorizing students to establish voting residences in their college communities, rebuking the refusal of [United States Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_General "United States Attorney General")[John N. Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_N._Mitchell "John N. Mitchell") the previous month to take a role in shaping voter registration laws as applicable to new voters.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-220) On December 24, 1971, Humphrey accused the Nixon administration of turning its back on the impoverished in the rural U.S., citing few implementations of the relief recommendations of the 1967 National Advisory Commission; in another statement he said only three of the 150 recommendations had been implemented.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-221) On December 27, responding to antiwar protesters in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), Humphrey said the Nixon administration was responsible for an escalation of the Southeast Asia war and requested complete cessation of North Vietnam bombing.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-222)

In January 1972, Humphrey said the U.S. would have been out of Vietnam by that point had he been elected president, saying Nixon was taking longer to withdraw American troops from the country than it took to defeat [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler").[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-223) On May 20, Humphrey said Nixon's proposal to limit schoolchildren busing was "insufficient in the amount of aid needed for our children, deceptive to the American people, and insensitive to the laws and the Constitution of this nation", in a reversal of his prior stance, while in [Milwaukee, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee,_Wisconsin "Milwaukee, Wisconsin").[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-224) During a May 30 appearance in [Burbank, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burbank,_California "Burbank, California"), Humphrey stated his support for an immediate withdrawal of American forces from South Vietnam despite an invasion by North Vietnam.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-225)

In January 1973, Humphrey said the Nixon administration was plotting to eliminate a school milk program in the upcoming fiscal year budget during a telephone interview.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-226) On February 18, 1973, Humphrey said the Middle East could possibly usher in peace following the Vietnam War ending along with American troops withdrawing from [Indochina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indochina "Indochina") during an appearance at the New York Hilton.[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-227) In August 1973, Humphrey called on Nixon to schedule a meeting with nations exporting and importing foods as part of an effort to both create a worldwide policy on food and do away with food hoarding.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-228) After Nixon's dismissal of [Archibald Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Cox "Archibald Cox"), Humphrey said he found "the whole situation entirely depressing."[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolberg1984449-229) Three days after Cox's dismissal, during a speech to the AFL-CIO convention on October 23, Humphrey declined to say whether he believed Nixon should be impeached, saying that his congressional position would likely cause him to play a role in determining Nixon's fate.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-230) On December 21, Humphrey disclosed his request of federal tax deductions of $199,153 for the donation of his vice-presidential papers to the Minnesota State Historical Society.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-231)

In early January 1974, Humphrey checked into the [Bethesda Naval Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethesda_Naval_Hospital "Bethesda Naval Hospital") for tests regarding a minute tumor of the bladder. His physician Edgar Berman said the next day that Humphrey "looks fine and feels fine" and was expected to leave early the following week.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-232) In an interview conducted on March 29, 1974, Humphrey concurred with Senator [Mike Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Mansfield "Mike Mansfield")'s assessment from the prior day that the House of Representatives had enough votes to impeach Nixon.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-233) Humphrey was reportedly pleased by Nixon's resignation.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-FOOTNOTESolberg1984449-229)

In an April 1975 news conference at the spring education conference of the United Federation of Teachers, Humphrey cited the need for a national department of education, a national education trust fund, and a federal government provision for a third of America's educational expenses. He said the Ford administration had no educational policy and noted the United States was the only industrialized country without a separate national education department.[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-234) In May, Humphrey testified at the trial of his former campaign manager Jack L. Chestnut, admitting that as a candidate he sought the support of Associated Milk Producers, Inc., but saying he was not privy to the illegal contributions Chestnut was accused of taking from the organization.[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-235) Later that month, Humphrey was one of 19 senators to originate a letter stating the expectation of 75 senators that Ford would submit a foreign aid request to Congress meeting the "urgent military and economic needs" of Israel.[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-236) In August, after the United States Court of Appeals ruled that Ford had no authority to continue levying fees of $2 a barrel on imported oil, Humphrey hailed the decision as "the best news we've heard on the inflation front in a long time" and urged Ford to accept the decision because the price reduction on oil and oil‐related products would benefit the national economy.[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-237) In October, after [Sara Jane Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Jane_Moore "Sara Jane Moore") attempted to assassinate Ford, Humphrey joined former presidential candidates Barry Goldwater, Edmund Muskie, and George McGovern in urging Ford and other presidential candidates to restrain their campaigning the following year to prevent future attempts on their lives.[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-238)

In October 1976, Humphrey was admitted to a hospital for the removal of a cancerous bladder,[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-239) predicted his victory in his reelection bid, and advocated for members of his party to launch efforts to increase voter turnout upon his release.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-240)

### 1972 presidential campaign

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Humphrey1972.gif/250px-Humphrey1972.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Humphrey1972.gif)

1972 campaign logo

On November 4, 1970, shortly after being reelected to the Senate, Humphrey stated his intention to take on the role of a "harmonizer" within the Democratic Party to minimize the possibility of potential presidential candidates within the party lambasting each other prior to deciding to run in the then-upcoming election, dismissing that he was an active candidate at that time.[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-241) In December 1971, Humphrey made his second trip to New Jersey in under a month, talking with a plurality of county leaders at the [Robert Treat Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Treat_Hotel "Robert Treat Hotel"): "I told them I wanted their support. I said I'd rather work with them than against them."[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-242)

In 1972, Humphrey once again ran for the [Democratic nomination for president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "1972 Democratic Party presidential primaries"), announcing his candidacy on January 10, 1972, during a twenty-minute speech in Philadelphia. At the time of the announcement, Humphrey said he was running on a platform of the removal of troops from Vietnam and a revitalization of the United States economy.[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-243) He drew upon continuing support from organized labor and the African-American and Jewish communities, but remained unpopular with college students because of his association with the Vietnam War, even though he had altered his position in the years since his 1968 defeat. Humphrey initially planned to skip the primaries, as he had in 1968. Even after he revised this strategy he still stayed out of New Hampshire, a decision that allowed McGovern to emerge as the leading challenger to Muskie in that state. Humphrey did win some primaries, including those in Ohio,[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-244) Indiana and Pennsylvania, but was defeated by McGovern in several others, including the crucial California primary. Humphrey also was out-organized by McGovern in caucus states and was trailing in delegates at the [1972 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Democratic_National_Convention "1972 Democratic National Convention") in [Miami Beach, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Beach,_Florida "Miami Beach, Florida"). His hopes rested on challenges to the credentials of some of the McGovern delegates. For example, the Humphrey forces argued that the winner-take-all rule for the California primary violated procedural reforms intended to produce a better reflection of the popular vote, the reason that the Illinois delegation was bounced. The effort failed, as several votes on delegate credentials went McGovern's way, guaranteeing his victory. After his primary win, McGovern asked Humphrey to be his running mate, but Humphrey declined.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Nixonland-2) After the election, Humphrey called Nixon and the two had an amicable conversation in which Humphrey implied that he preferred Nixon to McGovern, and had tried to keep McGovern from winning in [1972 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_United_States_presidential_election "1972 United States presidential election").[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-245)

### 1976 presidential election activities

On April 22, 1974, Humphrey said that he would not enter the upcoming [Democratic presidential primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "1976 Democratic Party presidential primaries") for the [1976 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_United_States_presidential_election "1976 United States presidential election"). Humphrey said at the time that he was urging fellow Senator and Minnesotan [Walter Mondale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Mondale "Walter Mondale") to run, despite believing that [Ted Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy "Ted Kennedy") would enter the race as well.[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-246) Leading up to the election cycle, Humphrey also said, "Here's a time in my life when I appear to have more support than at any other time in my life. But it's too financially, politically, and physically debilitating – and I'm just not going to do it."[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-247) In December 1975, a Gallup poll was released showing Humphrey and [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") as the leading Democratic and Republican candidates for the following year's presidential election.[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-248)

On April 12, 1976, Chairman of the [New Jersey Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Democratic_Party "New Jersey Democratic Party") State Senator James P. Dugan said the selection of a majority of uncommitted delegates could be interpreted as a victory for Humphrey, who had indicated his availability as a presidential candidate for the convention.[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-249) Humphrey announced his choice to not enter the New Jersey primary nor authorize any committees to work to support him during an April 29, 1976, appearance in the Senate Caucus Room.[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-250) Even after [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") had won enough delegates to clinch the nomination, many still wanted Humphrey to announce his availability for a [draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draft_(politics) "Draft (politics)"). However, he did not do so, and Carter easily secured the nomination on the first round of balloting. Humphrey had learned that he had terminal cancer, prompting him to sit the race out.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Humphrey attended the November 17, 1976, meeting between President-elect Carter and Democratic congressional leaders in which Carter sought out support for a proposal to have the president's power to reorganize the government reinstated with potential to be vetoed by Congress.[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-251)

### Fifth Senate term

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Hubert_Humphrey_in_his_Office_1976.jpg/250px-Hubert_Humphrey_in_his_Office_1976.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hubert_Humphrey_in_his_Office_1976.jpg)

Senator Humphrey in his office at the U.S. Capitol in 1976

Humphrey attended the May 3, 1977, White House meeting on legislative priorities. Humphrey told President Carter that the U.S. would enter a period of high unemployment without an economic stimulus and noted that in "every period in our history, a rise in unemployment has been accompanied by a rise in inflation". Humphrey stated a preventative health care program would be the only way for the Carter administration to not have to fund soaring health costs.[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-252) In July 1977, after the Senate began debating approval for funding of the [neutron bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_bomb "Neutron bomb"), Humphrey stated that the White House had agreed to release the impact statement, a requirement for congressional funding of a new weapon.[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-253)

### Deputy President pro tempore of the Senate (1977–1978)

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Humphrey_and_Carter.jpg/250px-Humphrey_and_Carter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Humphrey_and_Carter.jpg)

Senator Hubert Humphrey with President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") aboard [Air Force One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_One "Air Force One") in 1977

In 1974, along with [Rep. Augustus Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_F._Hawkins "Augustus F. Hawkins") of California, Humphrey authored the [Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey-Hawkins_Full_Employment_Act "Humphrey-Hawkins Full Employment Act"), the first attempt at full employment legislation. The original bill proposed to guarantee full employment to all citizens over 16 and set up a permanent system of public jobs to meet that goal. A watered-down version called the _Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act_ passed the House and Senate in 1978. It set the goal of 4 percent unemployment and 3 percent inflation and instructed the [Federal Reserve Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Board "Federal Reserve Board") to try to produce those goals when making policy decisions.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Humphrey ran for [Majority Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_leaders_of_the_United_States_Senate "Party leaders of the United States Senate") after the 1976 election but lost to [Robert Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Byrd "Robert Byrd") of [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia"). The Senate honored Humphrey by creating the post of [Deputy President pro tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_President_pro_tempore_of_the_United_States_Senate "Deputy President pro tempore of the United States Senate") of the Senate for him. On August 16, 1977, Humphrey revealed he was suffering from terminal [bladder cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bladder_cancer "Bladder cancer"). On October 25 of that year, he addressed the Senate, and on November 3, Humphrey became the first person other than a member of the House or the President of the United States to address the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") in session.[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-254) President Carter honored him by giving him command of [Air Force One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_One "Air Force One") for his final trip to Washington on October 23. One of Humphrey's final speeches contained the lines "It was once said that the moral test of Government is how that Government treats those who are in the dawn of life, the children; those who are in the twilight of life, the elderly; and those who are in the shadows of life, the sick, the needy and the handicapped",[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-255) which is sometimes described as the "liberals' mantra".

## Death and funeral

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/HumphreyGrave.jpg/250px-HumphreyGrave.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HumphreyGrave.jpg)

Burial plot of Hubert and Muriel Humphrey at [Lakewood Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakewood_Cemetery "Lakewood Cemetery") in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis")

Humphrey spent his last weeks calling old political acquaintances. One call was to Richard Nixon, inviting him to his upcoming funeral, which Nixon accepted. Staying in the hospital, Humphrey went from room to room, cheering up other patients by telling them jokes and listening to them. On January 13, 1978, he died of bladder cancer at his home in [Waverly, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waverly,_Minnesota "Waverly, Minnesota"), at the age of 66.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Humphrey's body [lay in state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lying_in_state#United_States "Lying in state") in the [rotundas of the U.S. Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol_rotunda "United States Capitol rotunda")[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-256) and the [Minnesota State Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_State_Capitol "Minnesota State Capitol") before being interred at [Lakewood Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakewood_Cemetery "Lakewood Cemetery") in Minneapolis. His death overshadowed the death of his colleague from [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"), Senator [Lee Metcalf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Metcalf "Lee Metcalf"), who had died the day before Humphrey. Old friends and opponents of Humphrey, from Gerald Ford and Richard Nixon to President Carter and Vice President Walter Mondale, paid their final respects. "He taught us how to live, and finally he taught us how to die", said Mondale.[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-257)

Humphrey's wife Muriel was appointed by Minnesota governor [Rudy Perpich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Perpich "Rudy Perpich") to serve in the U.S. Senate until a special election to fill the term was held; she did not seek election to finish her husband's term in office. In 1981, she married Max Brown and took the name Muriel Humphrey Brown.[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-258) Upon her death in 1998 she was interred next to Humphrey at Lakewood Cemetery.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-Mooar,_1998-31)

The epitaph on Humphrey's gravestone reads: "I have enjoyed my life, its disappointments outweighed by its pleasures. I have loved my country in a way that some people consider sentimental and out of style. I still do, and I remain an optimist, with joy, without apology, about this country and about the American experiment in democracy."[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Honors and legacy

In 1965, Humphrey was made an _Honorary Life Member_ of [Alpha Phi Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Phi_Alpha "Alpha Phi Alpha"), a historically African American fraternity.[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-259)

In 1978, Humphrey received the U.S. Senator John Heinz Award for Greatest Public Service by an Elected or Appointed Official, an award given out annually by [Jefferson Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Awards_for_Public_Service "Jefferson Awards for Public Service").[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-260)

He was awarded posthumously the [Congressional Gold Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Gold_Medal "Congressional Gold Medal") on June 13, 1979, and the [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom") in 1980.

He was honored by the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") with a 52¢ [Great Americans series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Americans_series "Great Americans series") (1980–2000) postage stamp.[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-261)

There is a statue of him in front of the Minneapolis City Hall.[[262]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-262)

Humphrey's legacy is bolstered by his early leadership in civil rights, and undermined by his long support of the Vietnam War. His leading biographer [Arnold A. Offner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_A._Offner "Arnold A. Offner") says he was "the most successful legislator in the nation's history and a powerful voice for equal justice for all."[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-263) Offner writes that Humphrey was:

> A major force for nearly every important liberal policy initiative....putting civil rights on his party's and the nation's agenda [in 1948] for decades to come. As senator he proposed legislation to effect national health insurance, for aid to poor nations, immigration and income tax reform, a Job Corps, the Peace Corps, the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency, and the path breaking 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty....[He provided] masterful stewardship of the historic 1964 Civil Rights Act through the Senate.[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-264)

While acknowledging his accomplishments, some historians emphasize that Humphrey was "a flawed, and not entirely likeable, figure who talked too much and neglected his family while pursuing a politics of compromise that owed as much to his vaunting personal ambition as to political pragmatism."[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey#cite_note-265)
